title: Satyabhama and the Syamantaka Mani
body:
Satyabhama and the Syamantaka Mani

Among the many legends of Lord Krishna, the tale of the Syamantaka Mani stands as one of intrigue, devotion, and divine justice. The Syamantaka was no ordinary jewel; it had been blessed by Surya, the Sun God, and produced gold each day and brought fortune to its owner. It belonged to Satrajit, the royal treasurer of Dwaraka and an ardent devotee of Surya, so radiant a gem that when Satrajit wore it the people mistook him for the Sun God himself.
Seeing its divine luster, Krishna advised Satrajit to offer the gem to King Ugrasena, so that its blessings might be shared by all. But Satrajit, blinded by greed, refused, and instead gave the jewel to his brother Prasena. Prasena wore it on a hunt deep into the forest, where a lion attacked and killed him and carried the gem away. Soon after, Jambavan, the mighty bear-king and devotee of Lord Rama, slew the lion and took the Syamantaka for himself, giving it to his child as a plaything.
When Prasena failed to return, rumors spread, and Satrajit, suspicious, accused Krishna of stealing the gem. Determined to clear His name, Krishna set out in search of it. Following Prasena's trail into the forest, He found the prince's remains and the tracks leading to Jambavan's cave, where the jewel gleamed in the hands of the bear-king's child. Mistaking Krishna for an intruder, Jambavan challenged Him, and the two fought a fierce duel that lasted twenty-one days. As the battle wore on, Jambavan began to falter, and marveling at his opponent's strength he realized that this was no ordinary warrior but his own Lord, the very Rama he had served in the Treta Yuga. Filled with devotion, he surrendered, and offered Krishna both the Syamantaka and his daughter Jambavati in marriage.
Krishna returned to Dwaraka with the gem and Jambavati, and presented the jewel to Satrajit. Overcome with guilt for his false accusation, Satrajit sought to make amends by offering Krishna both the gem and the hand of his daughter Satyabhama. Krishna accepted Satyabhama as His wife but declined the jewel, returning it to Satrajit. Yet the gem's fortune drew the envy of others, and a rival named Shatadhanva murdered Satrajit in his sleep and stole it. Enraged by her father's death, Satyabhama pleaded with Krishna to avenge him. Krishna and Balarama pursued Shatadhanva, who fled in fear; unable to escape, he left the gem with Akrura and continued his flight, but Krishna caught up with him and ended his life. When the jewel was not found on him, the search continued, until Krishna learned that Akrura held it. Understanding his devotion, Krishna allowed him to keep it, provided it remained in Dwaraka for the benefit of the Yadavas. Thus justice was restored, Krishna's name was cleared, and through the tale of the Syamantaka He gained His beloved wife Satyabhama.
